Logical Agents

Propositional Logic, First-Order Logic, Resolution

Agents that hold what they know as sentences, and work out what must follow from it.

Search finds a route. Logic derives a fact. A knowledge-based agent keeps what it believes in a knowledge base, and asks what necessarily follows from it. This is the foundation of expert systems, of formal safety checking, and of every system that must justify its answer instead of only producing one.

Learning objectives

  • Describe how a knowledge-based agent is built, and what TELL and ASK do.
  • Write sentences in propositional logic and evaluate them in a model.
  • Explain entailment, and check it with a truth table.
  • Convert sentences to CNF and prove a conclusion by resolution.
  • Express relations in first-order logic and apply unification.

Key terms in this module

Knowledge base (KB)
The set of sentences an agent currently believes to be true about its world.
TELL
The operation that adds a new sentence to the knowledge base.
ASK
The operation that asks the knowledge base what follows from what it holds.
Proposition say: prop-oh-ZISH-un
A statement that is either true or false, with no in-between: "the tank is full".
Propositional logic
A language built from propositions joined by not, and, or, implies, and if-and-only-if.
Model
One complete assignment of true or false to every proposition — one possible world.
Entailment say: en-TAIL-ment
KB ⊨ α means: in every model where the KB is true, α is also true. α follows necessarily.
Valid
True in every model, e.g. "P or not P". Also called a tautology.
Satisfiable say: SAT-is-fy-able
True in at least one model. Unsatisfiable means true in none.
Inference rule
A pattern that lets you derive a new sentence from existing ones, e.g. modus ponens.
Modus ponens say: MOH-dus POH-nens
From "A implies B" and "A", conclude "B".
Sound
An inference procedure is sound if everything it derives is actually entailed — it never invents falsehoods.
Complete
An inference procedure is complete if it can derive everything that is entailed — it never misses a conclusion. This is a different sense from Module 3, where a complete search algorithm is one that finds a solution whenever one exists.
CNF say: Conjunctive Normal Form
A sentence written as a set of clauses joined by AND, where each clause is a set of literals joined by OR.
Clause
An OR of literals, e.g. (¬A ∨ B ∨ C). A literal is a proposition or its negation.
Resolution
One inference rule that is complete for propositional logic: from two clauses containing P and ¬P, derive the clause made of everything else.
First-order logic (FOL)
Adds objects, relations, and the quantifiers ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists), so one sentence can describe many things at once.
Unification
Finding a substitution that makes two logical expressions identical, e.g. matching Teaches(x, AI4101) with Teaches(Ahmad, y).
Section 7.1

An agent that knows things

Every agent so far reacted to what it perceived, or searched for a path. A knowledge-based agent does something different: it stores facts, and it reasons about what those facts imply.

The agent keeps a knowledge base (KB): a set of sentences it believes. Two operations run it. TELL adds a new sentence. ASK asks what follows from everything in the KB. The reasoning happens inside ASK.

In the terms of Module 2, the knowledge base plays the role of the agent's internal state, written in logic.

A safety monitor in a factory

The system is TOLD the rules once: "if the pressure sensor is high and the valve is closed, there is a risk"; "if there is a risk and no operator has confirmed, sound the alarm".

Then it is TOLD the readings as they arrive: "pressure is high", "valve is closed". Nobody programmed a rule for this exact combination. The agent ASKs whether the alarm should sound, and the answer is derived, not looked up.

Why this design is worth the trouble

Add one new rule to the knowledge base and every conclusion that depends on it updates automatically, with no code changes. And the agent can show its work: "alarm, because risk, because pressure high and valve closed." Try getting that from a neural network. This explainability is why logic still runs in medical protocols, aircraft checks, tax rules, and formal verification of hardware.

4 min read

Section 7.2

Propositional logic: the smallest useful language

Start with the simplest logic there is. A proposition is a statement that is either true or false: PressureHigh, ValveClosed, AlarmOn.

The five connectives

Five symbols. Everything in propositional logic is built from them.
!
The one that confuses everyone: implies

"A ⇒ B" is true whenever A is false, no matter what B is. "If the moon is made of cheese, then I am the king" is a true sentence in logic. This feels wrong because everyday "if" suggests a cause. In logic there is no cause — only a promise: I only claim something when A holds. If A never holds, the promise was never broken.

Models and entailment

A model is one complete assignment of true/false to every proposition — one possible world. With n propositions there are 2n models. KB ⊨ α ("the KB entails α") means: in every model where the KB is true, α is also true.

Entailment is elimination, not calculation

Imagine every possible world laid out in a row. Each sentence you add to the KB crosses out the worlds where it is false. If, after crossing out, every world still standing has α true, then α follows — even if nobody ever stated it.

This gives a first inference method: truth table enumeration. List all 2n models, keep the ones where the KB is true, and check whether α is true in all of them. It is sound and complete — and completely impractical, because 30 propositions already mean a billion rows. The rest of this module is about doing better.

7 min read

Section 7.3

Inference: deriving new facts without listing worlds

Instead of checking every possible world, apply inference rules: patterns that take sentences you have and produce a sentence that must also be true.

  1. Modus ponens

    From A ⇒ B and A, derive B. This is the workhorse of every rule-based system.

  2. And-elimination

    From A ∧ B, derive A. Obvious, and used constantly.

  3. Contraposition

    A ⇒ B is the same sentence as ¬B ⇒ ¬A. If the alarm implies a fault, then no fault implies no alarm.

  4. De Morgan's laws

    ¬(A ∧ B) equals ¬A ∨ ¬B, and ¬(A ∨ B) equals ¬A ∧ ¬B. You need these to convert sentences later.

Two words you must not mix up

Sound

Everything derived is true

  • The procedure never invents a false conclusion
  • Without it, the agent's answers are worthless
  • "It only says true things"
Complete

Everything true can be derived

  • The procedure never misses a conclusion that follows
  • Without it, the agent may answer "I do not know" wrongly
  • "It says all the true things"
Sound matters more than complete

An unsound system tells you the patient is fine when they are not. An incomplete system says "I cannot determine that" when in fact it could. The first is dangerous; the second is merely limited. In practice we insist on soundness and accept whatever completeness we can afford.

A worked example

Knowledge base:

  • 1.

    PressureHigh ∧ ValveClosed ⇒ Risk

  • 2.

    Risk ∧ ¬OperatorConfirmed ⇒ Alarm

  • 3.

    PressureHigh

  • 4.

    ValveClosed

  • 5.

    ¬OperatorConfirmed

From 3 and 4 we have PressureHigh ∧ ValveClosed. With rule 1 and modus ponens: Risk. Combine with 5: Risk ∧ ¬OperatorConfirmed. With rule 2 and modus ponens: Alarm. Nobody wrote a rule for this exact situation, and the chain above is also the explanation the agent can show a human.

Section 7.4

CNF and resolution: one rule that does everything

Applying rules by hand works for five sentences. For a real knowledge base we want a single mechanical procedure. That is resolution — and it needs the sentences in a standard shape first.

Conjunctive Normal Form

A sentence is in CNF when it is a set of clauses joined by AND, where each clause is a set of literals joined by OR. A literal is a proposition or its negation. Every propositional sentence can be rewritten in CNF.

  1. Remove ⇔

    A ⇔ B becomes (A ⇒ B) ∧ (B ⇒ A).

  2. Remove ⇒

    A ⇒ B becomes ¬A ∨ B. This single step is worth memorising.

  3. Push ¬ inwards

    Use De Morgan's laws until every ¬ sits directly on a proposition.

  4. Distribute ∨ over ∧

    A ∨ (B ∧ C) becomes (A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ C).

The resolution rule

Take two clauses. If one contains P and the other contains ¬P, you may derive a new clause containing everything else from both. The pair cancels out.

Example: from (A ∨ B) and (¬B ∨ C) derive (A ∨ C).

Two witnesses, one contradiction

Witness one: "either Ahmad was there, or Badr was." Witness two: "if Badr was there, then the door was open." Put them together and something new follows: "either Ahmad was there, or the door was open." You have removed Badr from the picture — that is exactly what resolution does with P.

Proof by contradiction

Resolution is used in a particular way. To prove that the KB entails α:

  1. Add the opposite of what you want to prove

    Put ¬α into the knowledge base.

  2. Convert everything to CNF

    The whole KB plus ¬α.

  3. Resolve pairs repeatedly

    Each step produces a new clause; add it and continue.

  4. Look for the empty clause

    If two clauses P and ¬P resolve, the result contains nothing: a contradiction. That proves α must be true, because assuming it was false broke the world. If no new clauses can be produced and no contradiction appeared, α does not follow.

That procedure has a name worth knowing. A set of sentences is satisfiable if there is at least one model in which all of them are true, and unsatisfiable if there is none. So proving KB ⊨ α by contradiction is exactly proving that KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable — no possible world makes the knowledge base and the denial of α true together. The mirror idea is validity: a sentence is valid when it is true in every model, such as P ∨ ¬P.

i
Resolution is complete for propositional logic

One rule, applied mechanically, can prove anything that follows. That is a remarkable result, and it is why resolution — not a long list of rules — sits inside automated theorem provers and formal verification tools.

And notice what finding the proof actually is: you start from a set of clauses, generate new ones, and look for the empty clause. That is the frontier-and-expand loop of Module 3, with clauses in place of cities. Which clauses to resolve first is a heuristic question, exactly as it was there.

7 min read

Section 7.5

First-order logic: talking about things, not just facts

Propositional logic has a hard limit. To say "every student registered in AI4101 must sit the final exam", you would need one separate proposition for every student — and rewrite the knowledge base whenever someone registers.

First-order logic adds objects (Ahmad, AI4101, room 12), relations between them (Registered(Ahmad, AI4101)), functions (Advisor(Ahmad)), and two quantifiers: ∀ meaning "for all", and ∃ meaning "there exists".

One sentence replaces thousands

  • For all

    ∀x Registered(x, AI4101) ⇒ MustSitFinal(x) — covers every student, including the ones who register tomorrow.

  • There exists

    ∃x Teaches(x, AI4101) — somebody teaches this course, without saying who.

  • Both together

    ∀x ∃y Advises(y, x) — every student has some advisor. Order matters: swap the quantifiers and you claim one advisor advises everybody.

!
The two connectives that go with the two quantifiers

∀ almost always pairs with ⇒, and ∃ almost always pairs with ∧. Writing ∀x Registered(x, AI4101) ∧ MustSitFinal(x) claims that everything in the universe is registered in AI4101 — including this room and the moon. And ∃x Registered(x, AI4101) ⇒ MustSitFinal(x) is almost meaningless, because it is satisfied by anything that is not registered. This is the single most common mistake in first-order logic exams.

Unification: matching patterns

Unification finds a substitution that makes two expressions identical. Unifying Teaches(x, AI4101) with Teaches(Ahmad, y) gives {x = Ahmad, y = AI4101}. Unifying Teaches(x, AI4101) with Teaches(Ahmad, CS2107) fails — no substitution makes them equal.

Unification is what makes inference work in first-order logic. Resolution still applies, but now two clauses can be resolved when their literals unify rather than matching exactly. That extension is called lifted resolution, and it lets a single general rule fire on thousands of specific facts.

Where this ends up

Everything in this module runs today under different names. Database queries are first-order logic with a friendlier syntax. Prolog is resolution with unification as a programming language. Hospital protocol checkers, tax rule engines, aircraft configuration checks, and formal verification of chips are all knowledge bases plus an inference procedure. The vocabulary changes; the ideas are the ones on this page.

Check yourself

Write in first-order logic: "every student who passes AI4101 gets a certificate". Then say what goes wrong if you use ∧ instead of ⇒.

Show answer

∀x Passes(x, AI4101) ⇒ GetsCertificate(x). With ∧ it becomes ∀x Passes(x, AI4101) ∧ GetsCertificate(x), which says that everything that exists passes AI4101 and receives a certificate — every person, every chair, every planet. The sentence is not just wrong, it is false in any sensible world.

Revision card

Module 7 cheat sheet

Knowledge-based agent

  • KB = the sentences the agent believes
  • TELL adds a sentence · ASK queries what follows
  • New rules change every conclusion automatically — no code changes
  • The proof chain is the explanation you can show a human

Connectives

  • ¬A not · A ∧ B and · A ∨ B or (inclusive)
  • A ⇒ B false only when A true and B false
  • A ⇔ B true when both sides match
  • A ⇒ B ≡ ¬A ∨ B — memorise this

Key definitions

  • Model = one true/false assignment to all propositions (2ⁿ of them)
  • KB ⊨ α = α is true in every model where the KB is true
  • Valid = true in every model · satisfiable = true in at least one
  • Sound = derives only true things · complete = derives all true things

CNF in four steps

  • Remove ⇔ → two implications
  • Remove ⇒ → ¬A ∨ B
  • Push ¬ inwards with De Morgan
  • Distribute ∨ over ∧

Resolution

  • From (A ∨ B) and (¬B ∨ C) derive (A ∨ C)
  • To prove α: add ¬α, convert to CNF, resolve
  • Find the empty clause → contradiction → α is proved
  • Complete for propositional logic — one rule is enough

First-order logic

  • Adds objects, relations, functions, and quantifiers
  • ∀ goes with ⇒ · ∃ goes with ∧ — mixing them is the classic error
  • Quantifier order matters: ∀x ∃y ≠ ∃y ∀x
  • Unification matches patterns: Teaches(x, AI4101) + Teaches(Ahmad, y) → {x=Ahmad, y=AI4101}
